“I Can’t Get Started,” with music by Vernon Duke and lyrics by Ira Gershwin, was introduced in the 1936 Broadway production of *The Ziegfeld Follies*. Bob Hope and Eve Arden performed the song as a duet, presenting its witty catalogue of extraordinary accomplishments alongside the singer’s inability to begin a romance.

Trumpeter Bunny Berigan recorded the song with a small group later in 1936. The following year, he returned to it in an expansive big-band arrangement that featured his expressive trumpet playing and vocal. That 1937 recording became Berigan’s signature performance and helped establish “I Can’t Get Started” as a jazz standard. Billie Holiday recorded another notable interpretation soon afterward, accompanied by an ensemble led by Teddy Wilson and featuring Lester Young and several musicians associated with Count Basie’s orchestra. Their restrained, intimate treatment offered a striking contrast to Berigan’s dramatic version.

Singer Lee Wiley also had a personal connection to the song through Berigan, with whom she was briefly romantically involved and performed on radio. Despite that association, she recorded the ballad only once, in an informal performance at New York’s Town Hall in 1945.

One of Gershwin’s lyrics—“I’ve settled revolutions in Spain”—soon acquired an unexpected historical resonance. The song appeared in 1936, the same year the Spanish Civil War began; the conflict continued until 1939. “I Can’t Get Started,” with music by Vernon Duke and lyrics by Ira Gershwin, began life on Broadway in *Ziegfeld Follies of 1936*, where it was introduced by Bob Hope. Its elegant, wide-ranging melody and Gershwin’s witty lyric—an inventory of spectacular public accomplishments set against complete romantic failure—soon gave the song a life beyond the theater.

Trumpeter Bunny Berigan made the number his own. He recorded it more than once, and his celebrated late-1930s performance became both his signature recording and one of the defining ballad statements of the swing era. Berigan’s trumpet transformed the song’s urbane comedy into something more vulnerable and tragic, and he remained so closely associated with it that “I Can’t Get Started” virtually became his personal theme. Billie Holiday also recorded the song, bringing to it her characteristic intimacy and rhythmic freedom. In her hands, Gershwin’s polished declarations sounded less like clever exaggeration than a weary confession.

The song would seem to have been equally well suited to Lee Wiley. Her restrained delivery, sophisticated phrasing, and affinity for the great American songwriters made her an ideal interpreter of Duke and Gershwin’s blend of wit and melancholy. Wiley also performed the number with Berigan, a conjunction that promised a particularly natural balance between her cool vocal style and his emotionally charged trumpet. Yet, surprisingly, she never made a formal commercial recording of it. Her only known version was captured informally in 1945, leaving a tantalizing glimpse of how fully she could inhabit the song.

One line acquired an unintended historical force almost as soon as the number appeared: “I’ve settled revolutions in Spain.” Written as part of the singer’s fanciful list of worldly triumphs, it was originally a topical joke about international prestige and impossible achievement. But the Spanish Civil War began in 1936, the same year as the song’s Broadway debut, and continued with extraordinary violence until 1939. Against that reality, the lyric’s breezy boast became grimly ironic. A line designed to sound extravagantly comic was overtaken by events, adding another layer to a song already poised between sophistication, frustration, and heartbreak.

### Bunny Berigan: A Jazz Legend

Bunny Berigan was an influential American jazz trumpeter and bandleader of the 1930s. Celebrated for his powerful tone and expressive style, he performed with major artists such as Benny Goodman and Tommy Dorsey. His best-known recording, **“I Can’t Get Started,”** became a jazz standard and remains closely associated with him.

Although Berigan’s career was cut short by illness and alcoholism, his recordings show how deeply one musician can influence the development of jazz. His technical skill, emotional playing, and memorable solos continue to inspire trumpet players today.
